analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to fund worker pensions on par with their executive pension plans.
analysis.headline: A bill to require equitable pension funding for rank-and-file workers went nowhere in committee, drawing no cosponsors before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal pension law to require that, when a company runs pension plans for both executives and regular employees, the executive plans be funded no more than five percentage points better than the regular plans. It would also have required companies to put more money into underfunded worker pensions to close the gap. It was referred to committee and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Rank-and-file workers at companies that run pension plans for both ordinary employees and executives. If the bill passed, their pension plans could no longer be left underfunded while the company kept putting money into executive pensions; the gap would have to be closed within five percentage points or corrected with added contributions [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires that when an employer maintains both a non-executive pension plan and an executive pension plan, the executive plan's funded level cannot exceed the regular plan's by more than 5 percentage points
If the gap exceeds 5 percentage points, the employer must apply additional contributions to correct it by at least 5 percentage points, which would channel money into underfunded worker pensions

The bill's findings state that some large companies were setting aside millions to protect executive pensions while forgoing contributions to financially strained non-executive plans, and that underfunding of non-executive plans was increasing

The bill notes that companies must disclose details of employee pension plans in annual reports, but for executive pensions only the existence of trusts for the CEO and four other top executives, not the amounts in them, making the two plans hard to compare

analysis.who_pays: Corporations that maintain both regular employee pensions and executive pension plans. They would have to divert contributions from well-funded executive plans into underfunded rank-and-file plans whenever the executive plans were more than 5 percentage points better funded, and disclose more about those executive arrangements [S3].

drawbacks.text: The funding comparison is mechanically difficult: the bill's own findings acknowledge that executive pensions take many forms, including unfunded plans, rabbi trusts, and split-dollar life insurance, and that current disclosure rules do not reveal their funding levels, so enforcing a five-point comparison would be complicated
The rule applies only when a company maintains both types of plans, so companies could restructure or terminate their regular pension plans to avoid the requirement rather than fund them better
Employers would bear new compliance costs and might respond by cutting back executive plans or shifting to other forms of deferred compensation rather than increasing contributions to worker pensions

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: workers at companies with both kinds of pension plans would gain a guaranteed funding floor relative to executive plans, in a period when the bill's own findings documented growing underfunding of worker pensions. The main costs fall on employers, in the form of corrective contributions and compliance work, and the design has gaps — it does not cover companies without regular pension plans, and it relies on disclosure of executive plans that is currently very thin. On balance, the benefits to workers would outweigh the compliance costs if the enforcement mechanics could be made workable.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no one ever scheduled a hearing or vote, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. Doug Ose on May 13, 2003, and immediately referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce
It had no cosponsors in the House
On June 20, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, where it stayed
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded for the bill before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that fund executive pension plans while leaving their regular worker pensions underfunded, since they face no new funding or disclosure requirements. Workers' pensions remain subject to whatever contributions employers choose to make.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies funding executive pensions over worker pensions

for.name: Rep. Doug Ose
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: House committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Rep. John Boehner)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a markup or floor vote on the bill

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so no party-line split appears in the record; it had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party.

industries.industry: Corporations maintaining both employee and executive pension plans
industries.note: The bill would have forced companies maintaining executive pension plans to cap how much better funded those plans are than their regular worker plans, and to make corrective contributions. It died, so no new funding requirement took effect.

Executive compensation arrangements such as rabbi trusts, secular trusts, and split-dollar life insurance would have come under a new funding comparison. The bill also would have created compliance and disclosure work for the benefits and compensation field.
